text.p: Johan Cruyff raises a celebratory glass this Friday to what once seemed an unlikely 50th birthday.
A chain-smoker throughout a glittering soccer career, Cruyff was saved from premature death in 1991 by double by-pass heart surgery.
The then Barcelona coach subsequently lent his face to the city's anti-smoking campaign under the slogan: "Soccer gave me everything, but smoking nearly took it all away."
Cruyff's sacking from the Catalan club last year left a sour taste and this week he lost a legal battle against club president Jose Luis Nunez in which he had claimed defamation of character.
But he regularly appears on Dutch television and there are rumours of a managerial move to another big European club, possibly Real Madrid.
Cruyff's impending birthday has spawned a rash of coverage in the Dutch media, where he is still widely known as "the Saviour" -- an irreverent reference to his initials, JC.
An interview with the influential Dutch soccer magazine Voetball International betrays what is in effect his dual nationality.

Cruyff lists his favourite team strip as Ajax's red and white but his top stadium is Barcelona's Camp Nou. His favourite painter is Van Gogh, his favourite architect Gaudi. To relax, he listens to Nat King Cole and the Beatles, wears Hugo Boss clothes and cites "The Godfather" as his favourite film.

Born Hendrick Johannes Cruyff in the shadow of the former Ajax Amsterdam stadium De Meer, he signed as a 17-year-old for the club in 1964, donning for the first time the number "14" shirt he was to make his own. Lithe, wiry and strong, he turned into one of the most gifted footballers of his, or any, generation.
Television images of his trickery, bamboozling defenders with his close control, his deft flicks and agility will be broadcast as long as the game is played.
"A computer can't do in two minutes what a top footballer has to do in a hundreth of a second," he said in one interview published this week.
Cruyff was a slender figure who mesmerised opponents with speed and dazzling ball skills.
"Defenders could hardly play against him. If you watched his body instead of the ball you were lost. His body went everywhere," Ajax team mate Wim Suurbier recalled.
Cruyff was instrumental in taking Ajax to the top of the world game, and from 1971 helped to secure three successive European Cup titles for the Dutch Masters of "total football".
"Our football style of the '70s was one of controlled chaos," he commented.

In an international career spanning 48 appearances, Cryuff scored 33 goals. In 1974, he was chosen as "European Footballer of the Year" for the third time, a record that remains unbeaten alongside his 11 national titles as a player.
Single-minded and headstrong, Cruyff stunned the country in 1973 by announcing a move to Barcelona football club for what was then a world-record fee.
"The sale of Rembrandt's Night Watch could not have caused more dismay," one magazine said at the time.
His arrival marked a revival of fortunes at "Barca", helping them to win the Spanish league title in his first year.

However, in 1978, an unhappy 31-year-old Cruyff, who had lost much of his fortune in obscure business deals in Spain, announced he was quitting soccer. The lure of financial reward in the United States eventually proved too great, and he left to play with the Los Angeles Aztecs and then the Washington Diplomats.
Returning to Europe, he played briefly with Spain's Levante before rejoining Ajax in 1981 to win two more league titles and raise his goal tally for the club to 204 in 275 games.
After a year with rivals Feyenoord Rotterdam -- with whom he won the league -- he hung up his boots in May 1984, aged 37.
"I'm a professional. I can't say I'm tired and just play half a match. To me it's all or nothing," he said.
The following year, he was back at Ajax, this time as "technical director", and silverware duly followed. Ajax took the Dutch Cup in 1986 and 1987.

His return to his second love Barcelona as coach in 1988 marked the start of the club's second period of success, adding four national championships and two European Cups to the trophy cupboard. Throughout, Cruyff clung to his undying belief in football as entertainment.
"Wherever I go, I will always push for open attacking soccer, whatever the pressures," he once said.
Given his obvious talents and charisma -- the Dutch football association (KNVB) crowned him Player of the Century in 1989 -- it is surprising he was never given charge of the national team.
Even as a player Cruyff never held the World Cup.
In perhaps an unsporting tribute, one Dutch newspaper this week listed his top 10 career low-points.

The inventory includes being the first Dutchman ever to be sent off in an international (against Czechoslovakia in 1966), losing 8-0 to Bayern-Munich in a one-off friendly farewell game for Ajax in 1978 and, when playing for Feyenoord, losing 8-2 to his former Amsterdam club.
Not even a soccer legend is perfect.
